newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Alarm clocks ring "time up" for Bulgaria government.
newsitem.headline: Alarm clocks ring "time up" for Bulgaria government.

text.p: Students marched through Sofia on Monday with alarm clocks ringing to symbolise time running out for Bulgaria's Socialist rulers on the 14th day of protests against their plans to form a new government.
Drama and art school students turned out in costume. One girl dressed as death carried a sign saying: "I am the only one with a job in this country. Thank you BSP".

The Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) has offered elections by December, a year ahead of schedule, but is insisting on forming an interim cabinet to replace that of Zhan Videnov, who resigned on December 21.
Another poster depicted a cigarette and the warning "BSP is harmful to your health".
The daily students' protest gathered about 2,000 people and another 10,000 greeted by Gypsy musicians gathered at Sofia's Alexander Nevsky cathedral for the main opposition rally.
About 100 Gypsies piled onto several horse-drawn carts joined a procession to the cathedral.
Another group of demonstrators headed for national television to support a protest by staff there against government censorship.
Opposition protests received a boost on Sunday when opposition lawyer Petar Stoyanov was sworn in as president and said elections should be held as soon as possible.

"The 14th day of our protests is different because now we have a new legitimate president and this new president is going to be our guarantee for a victory at the coming elections," opposition Union of Democratic Forces leader Ivan Kostov told the rally.
"If they don't listen to us, they will have to oppose everybody, and this is a battle that they will never win. We shall never allow a second Socialist government to rule this country," he said.
Outgoing president Zhelyu Zhelev has refused to ask the Socialists to form a new government, a task likely to be inherited by Stoyanov when he takes office on Wednesday.

If the divided Socialists fail to do so, the president must ask the other parties in parliament, and if they fail or refuse, he appoints a caretaker government, dissolves parliament, and schedules elections within two months.
State radio said rallies took place in another eight towns around the country.

The Podkrepa trade union said one-hour warning strikes had taken place in several places including the Kremikovtsi steelworks, three mines near Pernik, the Pleven brewery and the shipbuilding yard at Bourgas. Token protests had also taken place among medical workers in Sofia, it said.
The Russian parliament issued a statement expressing concern over parallel protests against ex-communist governments in Bulgaria and Yugoslavia.

"The Douma is offering constructive cooperation to the parliaments and the socio-political forces of these countries to secure the stability of the Balkans and the future development of traditional relations and fruitful cooperation between Russia and the countries of this region," said a declaration carried by Bulgarian state news agency BTA.

At his swearing-in on Sunday, Stoyanov urged all parties to work together on measures to bring the country out of crisis, including a tough IMF-backed fixed exchange rate regime, greater financial discipline and a crackdown on corruption.

He met bankers, finance officials and other economic experts on Monday and sources at the meeting said the majority backed elections as soon as March to give a government with a firm mandate to negotiate with international lenders.
A new government is urgently needed to resume negotiations with the International Monetary Fund and avert default on Bulgaria's $10 billion foreign debt.

Incomes are now worth only a few dollars a month, fuelling demands for elections. The central bank fixed the lev currency for Tuesday at 731.71, sharply lower than the previous 682.12. It started the year at 495.74.
